[TODAY] Caught midair after 14 laps around Earth. 🚀

On Nov. 14, SpaceX's launch tower caught the upper stage of its Starship rocket with two giant arms as it came back from orbit. It is the first time this upper stage has been caught. During about 22.5 hours in space it circled Earth 14 times and released 26 Starlink satellites.

Why it matters: rockets that fly again, like airplanes, could make launches much cheaper.

Reality check: the booster missed its own catch and splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico. Refueling a ship in orbit, needed for Moon trips, has never been done.

[TODAY] Could you live 378 days without a window? 🔴

Four volunteers did. On Oct. 31 they stepped out of NASA's Mars Dune Alpha, a 3D-printed habitat of about 1,700 square feet in Houston, after 378 days inside. They had no windows or live calls home. Messages to the outside took up to 22 minutes each way, like on Mars.

They grew crops, drove a rover and a drone from inside, ran simulated Marswalks and tracked every supply down to dish soap. Their health data will help NASA plan its Moon Base and future Mars crews.

Reality check: this was a simulation on Earth, without space radiation or low gravity.

What would you miss most after a year inside? Tell us below.

[EMERGING] Why must Mars helicopters spin near sound speed? 🚁

Mars air is only 1% as dense as Earth's, so rotor blades must spin very fast to push enough of it down. NASA's Ingenuity helicopter kept its blade tips near Mach 0.7 to stay safely below the sound barrier.

In tests at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in a chamber filled with Mars-like air, new rotor tips reached Mach 1.08 without breaking. That adds about 30% more lift: room for science instruments or bigger batteries.

Reality check: this was a ground test. NASA's SkyFall concept aims to bring three next-gen helicopters to Mars in December 2028.

Save this for the next "how do you fly on Mars?" question.

[TODAY] An icy world hid beyond Pluto for years. 🪐

Astronomers found 2026 ED138 in early data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, while the telescope was still being tested. It sits about 46 times farther from the Sun than Earth does. Pluto averages 40.

Its size is estimated at 600 to 1,500 km, likely big enough to be round. Its team calls it the largest object found past Neptune in about 20 years. It hid near the crowded band of the Milky Way. Knowing where to look, they found it in images going back to 2016.

Reality check: it is still a candidate. Its true size needs more observations.

If it's confirmed, what should we name it? Tell us below.

[IMAGINE] A robot built a structure in orbit, alone. 🤖

What is real: Caltech's ASTRA robot, launched in March, pushed out two prebuilt sections of an antenna frame. Then it assembled a third from loose tubes and joints with no astronaut involved. Its team calls it the first structure built autonomously in space. Engineers could talk to it only 7 to 8 times a day for about 15 minutes, so they tested fixes on a twin robot in the lab.

Reality check: the planned 1.4 m antenna has 11 sections and will not be finished before the mission ends in December.

The speculation: what if giant telescopes too big for any rocket were built in orbit by robots?
